script.opening: (Anxious, tired, talking fast; baby can be heard in the background.) "Thanks for seeing me. I got a text saying my blood test was abnormal and to book — then I made the mistake of googling 'low platelets' at 2am with the baby. Now I'm convinced it's leukaemia. I've got a little one. I've been bruising on my legs and my gums bled brushing my teeth. Please just tell me straight — is it cancer?"

facts.text: "The bruises are on my shins — I don't remember knocking them." About three or four small bruises over two weeks. "The gums bled once when I was brushing." If asked: no nosebleeds, no blood in urine or stools, no tiny red spots she's noticed, no black stools, no bleeding into the eyes.
If asked: "No, none of that" — no fevers, night sweats, weight loss, bone pain or lumps in neck, armpits or groin. No recent infections. No headache.
"They're heavy — that's why I had the test. I didn't think much of it." Heavy since the baby, regular, 6–7 days, flooding on day 2. Last period ended a week ago.
"I'm tired, but I've got an eight-month-old." Not breathless, no palpitations.

No regular medicines; occasional paracetamol; no ibuprofen, aspirin, quinine or herbal remedies. "I don't think I'm pregnant, but I suppose I can't be completely sure" — condoms, not always. Stopped breastfeeding at 6 months. No allergies.
Platelets were normal in pregnancy as far as she knows. No liver disease. Drinks rarely. No family bleeding problems or blood disorders.
Lives with her partner, Sam, who works away Monday to Thursday. Her mum is 20 minutes away. Can get to the surgery or hospital today: "I can bring her — she'll probably sleep in the pram."

Frightened and apologetic: "Sorry, I'm just scared." If asked what she has read: "That low platelets and bruising are the first sign of leukaemia. And then I just kept thinking, who'd look after her?" Calms when the doctor explains that the rest of the blood count is normal. If told "it's nothing" with no plan, stay anxious. If asked to come in or have tests today: "Today? Is that because it's serious?" then accept once the reason is explained.

ice.ideas: "Low platelets and bruising — Google says leukaemia."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — that she has leukaemia and won't be there for her baby: "Who'd look after her?" Has hardly slept since the text.
ice.expectations: "Tell me it's not cancer. Or if it is, tell me now."

"I googled it at 2am." — ask what she read.
"Is that because it's serious?" — needs the reason for urgency explained calmly.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the result as an ISOLATED thrombocytopenia — explicitly checks that haemoglobin, white cells and film are otherwise normal — and recognises this most often means ITP, not leukaemia (which usually disturbs >1 line and/or shows blasts)
Confirms the count is genuine: requests/values a BLOOD FILM (± repeat) to exclude EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia and to look for blasts, abnormal cells and platelet morphology

Screens the SINISTER red flags (other cytopenias, blasts, B symptoms, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, significant/mucosal bleeding) on history and examination — and knows their presence triggers urgent/same-day haematology for suspected leukaemia (NICE NG12: adults — consider a very urgent FBC within 48 hours; a film suggesting leukaemia needs same-day haematology discussion); on video, arranges the examination face to face

Sets URGENCY BY THE NUMBER and bleeding (usual haematology practice; local pathways set exact thresholds): >50 vs 20–50 vs <20 / any significant bleeding (same-day) — and routes hers (38 with minor mucosal bleeding) to prompt urgent haematology rather than watchful waiting alone

Works the differential (ITP, post-viral, DRUGS, alcohol, a possible new pregnancy — gestational thrombocytopenia does not persist 8 months after delivery — HIV/hepatitis C, autoimmune) and gives BLEEDING PRECAUTIONS (avoid NSAIDs/aspirin/contact sport; urgent help for heavy bleeding, severe headache or neurological symptoms)
Meets the leukaemia fear with honesty — names the likely benign cause and why leukaemia is unlikely — WITHOUT false blanket reassurance and without feeding the 2am catastrophe
Communicates the plan to a frightened new mother clearly and warmly, checks understanding, and acknowledges the weight of having a young baby

Safety-nets robustly: bleeding red flags and when to seek same-day/emergency help, the referral and its timing, what tests come next, confirms she can repeat the plan, and arranges follow-up — owns and investigates the result, honest reassurance not blanket dismissal

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came, and I’m going to be straight with you because that’s what you asked for. Your platelets — the cells that help blood clot — are low, but importantly the rest of your blood count is normal. That pattern is much more likely to be a treatable immune problem than leukaemia."

"With leukaemia we’d almost always see other parts of the blood affected too — your red cells and infection-fighting cells — and we don’t. So while I’m taking this seriously and checking it properly, the thing you were up all night fearing is unlikely on these numbers."

"Two things I want to do. First, have the lab look at the blood under the microscope and repeat it — sometimes platelets clump and read falsely low. Second, let me ask about night sweats, weight loss, fevers and bone pain. … All clear — that’s genuinely reassuring. I can’t check for swollen glands or feel your tummy on video, so I’d like you to come in today or tomorrow for that, at the same time as the repeat blood test."

worked.lbl: Set the plan by the number
worked.txt: "Your count is low enough, with a bit of gum bleeding, that I don’t want to just watch it. I’m referring you to the blood specialists to be seen soon — they’ll confirm what’s going on and, if it’s the immune type, there are good treatments."

"While we wait: avoid ibuprofen and aspirin, and anything rough-and-tumble. If you get heavy bleeding that won’t stop, blood in your wee or stool, a severe headache, or any odd neurological symptoms, that’s an emergency — call 999 or go to A&E."

"You’ve got a little one and this fear makes total sense. Here’s what I want you to leave with: low platelets, rest of the count normal, most likely an immune cause, being seen by specialists quickly, and a clear plan if anything changes. I’ll chase the film and the referral and we’ll follow it through together."

f.learning: Interpreting an abnormal blood count safely starts with the PATTERN: an ISOLATED thrombocytopenia (platelets low, haemoglobin and white cells normal, no blasts on film) in a well young adult is most often IMMUNE THROMBOCYTOPENIA (ITP) — often post-viral or autoimmune — whereas leukaemia almost always disturbs more than one cell line and/or shows blasts. Confirm the count is genuine with a BLOOD FILM (± repeat) to exclude EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia and to inspect for blasts and abnormal cells. Screen the sinister pointers — other cytopenias, blasts, B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fevers), bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, significant/mucosal bleeding — whose presence triggers urgent or same-day haematology assessment for suspected leukaemia (NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026): in adults, consider a very urgent FBC within 48 hours for features that could suggest leukaemia; immediate specialist referral for petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly is the children and young people recommendation). Examination for nodes and organomegaly cannot be done on video — arrange it face to face. Set urgency by the count and bleeding (usual haematology practice; local pathways set exact thresholds): >50 with no bleeding can be investigated in primary care and referred routinely/urgently; 20–50 warrants urgent haematology; <20, any significant bleeding, or systemic illness needs same-day assessment/admission. Work the differential (ITP, post-viral, drugs, alcohol, a possible new pregnancy — not gestational thrombocytopenia 8 months after delivery — HIV/hepatitis C, autoimmune) and give bleeding precautions (avoid NSAIDs/aspirin/contact sport; emergency help for heavy bleeding, severe headache or neurological symptoms). The communication core is a frightened new mother’s 2am leukaemia terror: meet it with honesty and the most likely explanation WITHOUT false blanket reassurance, set a clear plan and safety-net, and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: International consensus report on immune thrombocytopenia (Provan et al., Blood Advances 2019) (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Good Medical Practice (2024)
knowledge.summary: A platelet count of 38 with a normal haemoglobin and white count, in a well 27-year-old, is an isolated thrombocytopenia — most often immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), not leukaemia. Confirm it with a film, screen for red flags, examine her in person, and get prompt haematology advice because she has mucosal bleeding.

points.t: Only one cell line is low. Leukaemia usually disturbs more than one line or shows abnormal cells on the film. Isolated thrombocytopenia in a well young adult is most often ITP, which is a diagnosis of exclusion (Provan et al. 2019, international).

points.h: Make sure the number is real
points.t: EDTA can make platelets clump and read falsely low (pseudothrombocytopenia). A blood film, and a repeat in a citrate tube if clumping is seen, confirms a true low count and looks for blasts, red-cell fragments and giant platelets.

NICE NG12: in adults, consider a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) to assess for leukaemia if there is pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, persistent or recurrent infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, unexplained bruising, bleeding or petechiae, or hepatosplenomegaly. She already has the count; the film and examination are the next step. A film suggesting acute leukaemia needs same-day discussion with haematology (clinical practice; NICE NG12’s immediate-specialist-assessment recommendation for unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly applies to children and young people).

In usual haematology practice, a count below 20, active or significant bleeding, blasts or fragments on the film, or a systemically unwell patient means same-day assessment. A new, unexplained count below 50 — as here, with minor mucosal bleeding — needs same-day haematology advice rather than a routine wait. Local pathways set the exact thresholds.

Recent viral illness, medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal), alcohol, pregnancy, autoimmune disease (joint pain, rashes), and infections that cause ITP such as HIV and hepatitis C, which the international consensus advises testing for in adults. Her heavy periods may be a result of the low platelets rather than a separate problem.

Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, which impair platelet function (BNF). Avoid contact sport. Heavy bleeding that won’t stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, a severe headache or new neurological symptoms need emergency care.

Eight-month-old baby, sleep deprivation, childcare for an in-person visit, who is at home to support her.

ITP vs pseudothrombocytopenia vs post-viral vs drugs or alcohol vs pregnancy vs autoimmune vs marrow disease; heavy periods as a consequence, not a separate problem.
Screened B symptoms, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, infections, petechiae and significant bleeding; knew other cytopenias or blasts would change the plan (NICE NG12 leukaemia criteria).
Isolated thrombocytopenia, most likely ITP; leukaemia unlikely but not excluded until the film and specialist review.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

model.text: Hello Chloe, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me okay, and is now a good time to talk? … You said in your message you’re worried. Tell me what’s been going on.
model.why: Checks the video set-up and opens with her agenda

model.text: I got a text saying my blood test was abnormal. Then I googled low platelets at 2am with the baby and now I’m convinced it’s leukaemia. I’ve been bruising on my legs and my gums bled. Please just tell me straight — is it cancer?

I will be straight with you, I promise. The short answer first: your platelets are low, but the rest of your blood count is normal, and that pattern is much more often a treatable immune problem than leukaemia. I want to check a few things to be sure. Is it okay if I ask some questions and then we plan together?
model.why: Answers the direct question honestly and early, without blanket reassurance

model.text: Okay. Yes. Sorry, I’m just scared.
There’s nothing to be sorry for. Tell me about the bruising and the gums.
model.why: Opens the bleeding history

model.text: The bruises are on my shins — I don’t remember knocking them. The gums bled once when I was brushing.
Any tiny red or purple pinprick spots on your skin, nosebleeds, blood in your wee or your poo, or black stools?
model.why: Screens for petechiae and more significant bleeding

model.text: No, none of that. Just the bruises and the gums that one time.
And the periods — the test was done for heavy periods. How heavy, and have you been flooding or passing clots?
model.why: Links the heavy periods to the low platelets

model.text: They’re heavy — that’s why I had the test. I didn’t think much of it.

That may well be connected — low platelets can make periods heavier. Now some questions to make sure we’re not missing anything more serious: any night sweats that soak the sheets, fevers, weight loss you can’t explain, bone pain, lumps in your neck, armpits or groin, or lots of infections?
model.why: Screens the red flags for leukaemia and lymphoma

model.text: No. I’m tired, but I’ve got an eight-month-old.
Any recent cold, flu or tummy bug? And could you be pregnant at all?
model.why: Explores post-viral and pregnancy causes

model.text: Nothing I can think of. I don’t think I’m pregnant, but I suppose I can’t be completely sure.

That’s fine — we can check. I’ll also go through any medicines, remedies or supplements with you, including anything bought over the counter, because some can lower platelets. We’ll talk about alcohol too — it can affect platelets.
model.why: Covers drugs and alcohol without inventing an answer

model.text: Okay, that’s fine.

Can you show me the bruises on your shins on the camera? … Thank you. They look like ordinary bruises, but a camera can’t replace an examination — I want to see you in person to look properly for glands, check your tummy and examine your skin.
model.why: Uses the video usefully and recognises its limits

model.text: What was it you read at 2am that frightened you most?
model.why: Explores the idea behind the fear

model.text: That low platelets and bruising are the first sign of leukaemia. And then I just kept thinking, who’d look after her?
That’s a terrifying thought to have alone in the middle of the night with a baby. Thank you for telling me. What were you hoping I’d do today?
model.why: Acknowledges the emotion and elicits expectations

model.text: Tell me it’s not cancer. Or if it is, tell me now.

Here’s what I know. Leukaemia almost always affects the other parts of the blood too — the red cells and the infection-fighting cells — and yours are normal, and the lab saw no abnormal cells. You have no night sweats, weight loss, fevers or bone pain. So leukaemia is unlikely. The most likely cause is immune thrombocytopenia — your immune system clearing platelets too quickly, sometimes after a virus. I can’t promise anything until the film and the specialists have looked, and I won’t pretend otherwise.
model.why: Gives a working diagnosis and honest probability

model.text: So it’s probably not leukaemia?

Probably not, on everything we have. But because your count is 38 and your gums have bled, I don’t want to simply watch and wait. I’ll ring the haematology team today for advice, and I’d like a repeat count and a blood film done today or tomorrow — the film lets the lab look at the cells under a microscope and check the low number isn’t just clumping in the tube.
model.why: Sets urgency by count and bleeding; confirms the count is genuine

model.text: Today? Is that because it’s serious?

It’s because it matters, not because I think it’s cancer. At this level you’re unlikely to have a serious bleed, but I want the specialists involved promptly so we get an answer quickly. They’ll probably also check things like a virus screen, including HIV and hepatitis C — that’s routine for anyone with this result, not a judgement.
model.why: Explains urgency without alarming and normalises routine tests

model.text: Okay. That makes sense.
Can you come in to the surgery today so I can examine you and we take the bloods at the same time? Is there someone who can have the baby, or would you like to bring her?
model.why: Arranges the in-person examination and problem-solves childcare

model.text: I can bring her — she’ll probably sleep in the pram.
Perfect. Until we know more: no ibuprofen or aspirin — paracetamol is fine for pain. Avoid anything rough-and-tumble. Brush your teeth with a soft brush. And a pregnancy test when you come in.
model.why: Bleeding precautions and pregnancy check

model.text: Okay. What about my periods — they’re heavy.

Good question. I’ll ask haematology about that when I call, as there are treatments that help and some are better than others when platelets are low. If you soak through a pad or tampon every hour for a couple of hours, that needs urgent help.
model.why: Addresses the heavy periods as linked to thrombocytopenia

model.text: Now the important part. If you get bleeding that won’t stop after ten minutes of pressure, blood in your wee or poo, black stools, vomiting blood, a sudden severe headache, confusion or weakness, or a rash of tiny red spots spreading — call 999 or go straight to A&E, and say your platelets are low.
model.why: Specific emergency safety-net in plain language

model.text: Okay. That’s scary but I get it.
It is unlikely, but I want you to know exactly what to do. Just so I know I’ve explained it well, if you were explaining this to someone at home tonight, what would you say?
model.why: Checks understanding with teach-back, neutral about who is at home

model.text: That my platelets are low but the rest of my blood is normal, so it’s probably an immune thing, not leukaemia. I’m coming in today for an examination and more tests, the doctor is calling the specialists, and no ibuprofen.

That’s exactly it. I’ll phone you myself with the film result and what haematology say, and I’ll stay involved until we have an answer. Please don’t google at 2am — ring us instead. Anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Owns the result, sets follow-up and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thank you — I actually feel like I can breathe.

social.t: Sleep deprivation with a young baby and a 2am online search amplify fear. Practical help — bringing the baby to appointments, who can support her — makes the plan workable.
She found worst-case content first. Offer reliable sources and a direct route back to the practice so she isn’t left searching alone.

legal.t: Seeking haematology advice and making a referral share her data for direct care; explain this and record her agreement. She can bring a companion to appointments.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): follow up results you request and act on them. A text asking her to book is not a plan — make sure the film, haematology advice and follow-up actually happen and are recorded.
An examination for lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and petechiae cannot be done on video. Recognise it and arrange a face-to-face assessment promptly.

community.t: The ITP Support Association provides patient information once a diagnosis is confirmed; health visitor and family support for the practicalities of appointments with a baby.

Count below 20, or systemically unwell — same-day assessment

playbook.diagnosis: An isolated thrombocytopenia (platelets 38, haemoglobin and white cells normal, no blasts flagged) in a well young woman — most likely immune thrombocytopenia. Leukaemia is unlikely but not excluded until the film and haematology review.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Platelets are the tiny cells that help blood clot. Yours are low, but your red cells and infection-fighting cells are normal. When only platelets are low like this, the usual cause is the immune system clearing them too quickly — it’s treatable. Leukaemia nearly always upsets the other cells too.”

management.reflectIce: “You were up at 2am thinking about who would look after your little girl. I want to give you real answers quickly, which is why I’m acting today.”
management.psychosocial: Make the plan work with a baby: bring her to the appointment, one visit for examination and bloods, and a named person (you) phoning back so she isn’t left waiting and searching.
sharedPlan: Blood film and repeat count today or tomorrow (citrate tube if clumping); pregnancy test
Face-to-face examination today for nodes, liver, spleen and skin
Haematology advice today because of count 38 with gum bleeding; further tests (such as HIV and hepatitis C) as they advise
Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin and contact sport; paracetamol if needed; ask haematology about treating the heavy periods
safetyNet: 999 or A&E: bleeding that won’t stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, vomiting blood, severe headache, confusion or weakness
GP phones back with the film and haematology plan; follow up until a diagnosis is made

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can interpret a result safely and tell a frightened patient the truth. Candidates fail by alarming her, by dismissing her, or by choosing the wrong urgency for a count of 38 with bleeding.

items.fail: Treating any low platelet count as possible leukaemia and saying so first.
items.why: Ignores the pattern. Normal haemoglobin and white cells with no blasts makes ITP far more likely; leading with leukaemia confirms her 2am fear.
items.fix: Read the whole count aloud in plain words — “only the platelets are low” — and say what that pattern usually means.

items.fail: Planning a repeat FBC in a month and nothing else.
items.why: A count of 38 with gum bleeding needs prompt haematology advice and a film. Watchful waiting alone is unsafe.
items.fix: Film and repeat now, haematology advice today, and bleeding precautions while waiting.

items.fail: Doing the “examination” on video and declaring no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
items.why: You can’t palpate nodes or a spleen through a camera. Examiners mark down claims that can’t be true.
items.fix: Look at the bruises on screen, then say you need to examine her in person today — and arrange it.

items.why: False blanket reassurance before the film and examination. It is unsafe and patients recognise it.
items.fix: Honest probability: “Everything so far points away from leukaemia, and here is how we’ll confirm that.”

items.fail: Brushing past the baby and the 2am search to get to the questions.
items.why: The fear for her baby is the hidden agenda. Missing it costs Relating to Others marks and she won’t hear your explanation.
items.fix: “What did you read that frightened you most?” — then name the fear before you explain.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if you’re worried.”
items.why: Non-specific. With platelets of 38 she needs to know exactly which bleeding symptoms are an emergency.
items.fix: Name them: bleeding that won’t stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, severe headache, confusion or weakness — 999 or A&E.

items.fail: Forgetting the heavy periods that prompted the test.
items.why: Low platelets may be causing them, and they are a bleeding risk. Missing the link looks like a checklist history.
items.fix: Ask about flooding and clots, link it to the platelets, and ask haematology how best to treat it.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: answers “is it cancer?” honestly in the first minute; explains why leukaemia is unlikely in words she can repeat; recognises the video can’t replace an examination and gets her seen today; links the heavy periods to the low platelets; problem-solves bringing the baby; teach-back; owns the result by phoning her back personally.

avoid.dont: “You’ve got idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, we’ll need to exclude pseudothrombocytopenia.”
avoid.instead: “Your immune system may be clearing platelets too fast. I also want to check the machine didn’t miscount because they clumped in the tube.”
avoid.why: Jargon increases fear and loses Relating to Others marks.

SCA_MODELS.text: Hello Chloe, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me okay, and is now a good time to talk? … You said in your message you’re worried. Tell me what’s been going on.
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks the video set-up and opens with her agenda

SCA_MODELS.text: I got a text saying my blood test was abnormal. Then I googled low platelets at 2am with the baby and now I’m convinced it’s leukaemia. I’ve been bruising on my legs and my gums bled. Please just tell me straight — is it cancer?

I will be straight with you, I promise. The short answer first: your platelets are low, but the rest of your blood count is normal, and that pattern is much more often a treatable immune problem than leukaemia. I want to check a few things to be sure. Is it okay if I ask some questions and then we plan together?
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers the direct question honestly and early, without blanket reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Yes. Sorry, I’m just scared.
There’s nothing to be sorry for. Tell me about the bruising and the gums.
SCA_MODELS.why: Opens the bleeding history

SCA_MODELS.text: The bruises are on my shins — I don’t remember knocking them. The gums bled once when I was brushing.
Any tiny red or purple pinprick spots on your skin, nosebleeds, blood in your wee or your poo, or black stools?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for petechiae and more significant bleeding

SCA_MODELS.text: No, none of that. Just the bruises and the gums that one time.
And the periods — the test was done for heavy periods. How heavy, and have you been flooding or passing clots?
SCA_MODELS.why: Links the heavy periods to the low platelets

SCA_MODELS.text: They’re heavy — that’s why I had the test. I didn’t think much of it.

That may well be connected — low platelets can make periods heavier. Now some questions to make sure we’re not missing anything more serious: any night sweats that soak the sheets, fevers, weight loss you can’t explain, bone pain, lumps in your neck, armpits or groin, or lots of infections?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens the red flags for leukaemia and lymphoma

SCA_MODELS.text: No. I’m tired, but I’ve got an eight-month-old.
Any recent cold, flu or tummy bug? And could you be pregnant at all?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores post-viral and pregnancy causes

SCA_MODELS.text: Nothing I can think of. I don’t think I’m pregnant, but I suppose I can’t be completely sure.

That’s fine — we can check. I’ll also go through any medicines, remedies or supplements with you, including anything bought over the counter, because some can lower platelets. We’ll talk about alcohol too — it can affect platelets.
SCA_MODELS.why: Covers drugs and alcohol without inventing an answer

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay, that’s fine.

Can you show me the bruises on your shins on the camera? … Thank you. They look like ordinary bruises, but a camera can’t replace an examination — I want to see you in person to look properly for glands, check your tummy and examine your skin.
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses the video usefully and recognises its limits

SCA_MODELS.text: What was it you read at 2am that frightened you most?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the idea behind the fear

SCA_MODELS.text: That low platelets and bruising are the first sign of leukaemia. And then I just kept thinking, who’d look after her?
That’s a terrifying thought to have alone in the middle of the night with a baby. Thank you for telling me. What were you hoping I’d do today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the emotion and elicits expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: Tell me it’s not cancer. Or if it is, tell me now.

Here’s what I know. Leukaemia almost always affects the other parts of the blood too — the red cells and the infection-fighting cells — and yours are normal, and the lab saw no abnormal cells. You have no night sweats, weight loss, fevers or bone pain. So leukaemia is unlikely. The most likely cause is immune thrombocytopenia — your immune system clearing platelets too quickly, sometimes after a virus. I can’t promise anything until the film and the specialists have looked, and I won’t pretend otherwise.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives a working diagnosis and honest probability

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s probably not leukaemia?

Probably not, on everything we have. But because your count is 38 and your gums have bled, I don’t want to simply watch and wait. I’ll ring the haematology team today for advice, and I’d like a repeat count and a blood film done today or tomorrow — the film lets the lab look at the cells under a microscope and check the low number isn’t just clumping in the tube.
SCA_MODELS.why: Sets urgency by count and bleeding; confirms the count is genuine

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? Is that because it’s serious?

It’s because it matters, not because I think it’s cancer. At this level you’re unlikely to have a serious bleed, but I want the specialists involved promptly so we get an answer quickly. They’ll probably also check things like a virus screen, including HIV and hepatitis C — that’s routine for anyone with this result, not a judgement.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains urgency without alarming and normalises routine tests

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That makes sense.
Can you come in to the surgery today so I can examine you and we take the bloods at the same time? Is there someone who can have the baby, or would you like to bring her?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges the in-person examination and problem-solves childcare

SCA_MODELS.text: I can bring her — she’ll probably sleep in the pram.
Perfect. Until we know more: no ibuprofen or aspirin — paracetamol is fine for pain. Avoid anything rough-and-tumble. Brush your teeth with a soft brush. And a pregnancy test when you come in.
SCA_MODELS.why: Bleeding precautions and pregnancy check

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. What about my periods — they’re heavy.

Good question. I’ll ask haematology about that when I call, as there are treatments that help and some are better than others when platelets are low. If you soak through a pad or tampon every hour for a couple of hours, that needs urgent help.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the heavy periods as linked to thrombocytopenia

SCA_MODELS.text: Now the important part. If you get bleeding that won’t stop after ten minutes of pressure, blood in your wee or poo, black stools, vomiting blood, a sudden severe headache, confusion or weakness, or a rash of tiny red spots spreading — call 999 or go straight to A&E, and say your platelets are low.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific emergency safety-net in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s scary but I get it.
It is unlikely, but I want you to know exactly what to do. Just so I know I’ve explained it well, if you were explaining this to someone at home tonight, what would you say?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks understanding with teach-back, neutral about who is at home

SCA_MODELS.text: That my platelets are low but the rest of my blood is normal, so it’s probably an immune thing, not leukaemia. I’m coming in today for an examination and more tests, the doctor is calling the specialists, and no ibuprofen.

That’s exactly it. I’ll phone you myself with the film result and what haematology say, and I’ll stay involved until we have an answer. Please don’t google at 2am — ring us instead. Anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Owns the result, sets follow-up and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you — I actually feel like I can breathe.

SCA_STEM.name: Chloe Fenner
pmh: Heavy periods and tiredness (reason for recent blood test)
SCA_STEM.recent: FBC last week for heavy periods and tiredness: platelets 38 × 10⁹/L. Haemoglobin normal, white cell count normal, no blasts flagged by the lab. No previous platelet count on record. Text sent asking her to book.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss an abnormal blood count.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: International consensus report on immune thrombocytopenia (Provan et al., Blood Advances 2019) (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Good Medical Practice (2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A platelet count of 38 with a normal haemoglobin and white count, in a well 27-year-old, is an isolated thrombocytopenia — most often immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), not leukaemia. Confirm it with a film, screen for red flags, examine her in person, and get prompt haematology advice because she has mucosal bleeding.

points.t: Only one cell line is low. Leukaemia usually disturbs more than one line or shows abnormal cells on the film. Isolated thrombocytopenia in a well young adult is most often ITP, which is a diagnosis of exclusion (Provan et al. 2019, international).

points.h: Make sure the number is real
points.t: EDTA can make platelets clump and read falsely low (pseudothrombocytopenia). A blood film, and a repeat in a citrate tube if clumping is seen, confirms a true low count and looks for blasts, red-cell fragments and giant platelets.

NICE NG12: in adults, consider a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) to assess for leukaemia if there is pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, persistent or recurrent infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, unexplained bruising, bleeding or petechiae, or hepatosplenomegaly. She already has the count; the film and examination are the next step. A film suggesting acute leukaemia needs same-day discussion with haematology (clinical practice; NICE NG12’s immediate-specialist-assessment recommendation for unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly applies to children and young people).

In usual haematology practice, a count below 20, active or significant bleeding, blasts or fragments on the film, or a systemically unwell patient means same-day assessment. A new, unexplained count below 50 — as here, with minor mucosal bleeding — needs same-day haematology advice rather than a routine wait. Local pathways set the exact thresholds.

Recent viral illness, medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal), alcohol, pregnancy, autoimmune disease (joint pain, rashes), and infections that cause ITP such as HIV and hepatitis C, which the international consensus advises testing for in adults. Her heavy periods may be a result of the low platelets rather than a separate problem.

Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, which impair platelet function (BNF). Avoid contact sport. Heavy bleeding that won’t stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, a severe headache or new neurological symptoms need emergency care.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her voice the leukaemia fear; answered “is it cancer?” honestly early rather than deferring it to the end.
Eight-month-old baby, sleep deprivation, childcare for an in-person visit, who is at home to support her.
Picked up the bruising and gum bleeding, the heavy periods and the 2am search, and explored each.
Idea (leukaemia from an online search); concern (not being there for her baby); expectation (a straight answer today).
Blood film and repeat (citrate if clumping); in-person examination for nodes, spleen, liver and skin; pregnancy test; haematology to guide further tests such as HIV and hepatitis C.
ITP vs pseudothrombocytopenia vs post-viral vs drugs or alcohol vs pregnancy vs autoimmune vs marrow disease; heavy periods as a consequence, not a separate problem.
Screened B symptoms, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, infections, petechiae and significant bleeding; knew other cytopenias or blasts would change the plan (NICE NG12 leukaemia criteria).
Isolated thrombocytopenia, most likely ITP; leukaemia unlikely but not excluded until the film and specialist review.
Same-day haematology advice given the count and mucosal bleeding; film and repeat today or tomorrow; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin; honest, not blanket, reassurance.
Heavy periods managed with haematology input; medicines and supplements reviewed; pregnancy excluded.
Named emergency symptoms (uncontrolled bleeding, blood in urine or stool, severe headache, neurology); GP phones back with results; teach-back.

social.t: Sleep deprivation with a young baby and a 2am online search amplify fear. Practical help — bringing the baby to appointments, who can support her — makes the plan workable.
She found worst-case content first. Offer reliable sources and a direct route back to the practice so she isn’t left searching alone.

legal.t: Seeking haematology advice and making a referral share her data for direct care; explain this and record her agreement. She can bring a companion to appointments.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): follow up results you request and act on them. A text asking her to book is not a plan — make sure the film, haematology advice and follow-up actually happen and are recorded.
An examination for lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and petechiae cannot be done on video. Recognise it and arrange a face-to-face assessment promptly.

community.t: The ITP Support Association provides patient information once a diagnosis is confirmed; health visitor and family support for the practicalities of appointments with a baby.

redFlags: Other cytopenias or blasts on the film — suspected leukaemia; immediate referral
Drenching night sweats, fevers, weight loss, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent infections
Significant bleeding (not stopping, blood in urine or stool, melaena), severe headache or new neurology — emergency
Count below 20, or systemically unwell — same-day assessment
psychosocial: Eight-month-old baby — sleep, support at home, childcare for appointments
The 2am search and the fear it produced
ice: Idea: “Low platelets and bruising mean leukaemia”
Concern: not being there for her baby
Expectation: a straight answer today — is it cancer?

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: An isolated thrombocytopenia (platelets 38, haemoglobin and white cells normal, no blasts flagged) in a well young woman — most likely immune thrombocytopenia. Leukaemia is unlikely but not excluded until the film and haematology review.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Platelets are the tiny cells that help blood clot. Yours are low, but your red cells and infection-fighting cells are normal. When only platelets are low like this, the usual cause is the immune system clearing them too quickly — it’s treatable. Leukaemia nearly always upsets the other cells too.”

management.reflectIce: “You were up at 2am thinking about who would look after your little girl. I want to give you real answers quickly, which is why I’m acting today.”
management.psychosocial: Make the plan work with a baby: bring her to the appointment, one visit for examination and bloods, and a named person (you) phoning back so she isn’t left waiting and searching.

Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin and contact sport; paracetamol if needed; ask haematology about treating the heavy periods

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can interpret a result safely and tell a frightened patient the truth. Candidates fail by alarming her, by dismissing her, or by choosing the wrong urgency for a count of 38 with bleeding.

items.fail: Treating any low platelet count as possible leukaemia and saying so first.
items.why: Ignores the pattern. Normal haemoglobin and white cells with no blasts makes ITP far more likely; leading with leukaemia confirms her 2am fear.
items.fix: Read the whole count aloud in plain words — “only the platelets are low” — and say what that pattern usually means.

items.fail: Planning a repeat FBC in a month and nothing else.
items.why: A count of 38 with gum bleeding needs prompt haematology advice and a film. Watchful waiting alone is unsafe.
items.fix: Film and repeat now, haematology advice today, and bleeding precautions while waiting.

items.fail: Doing the “examination” on video and declaring no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
items.why: You can’t palpate nodes or a spleen through a camera. Examiners mark down claims that can’t be true.
items.fix: Look at the bruises on screen, then say you need to examine her in person today — and arrange it.

items.why: False blanket reassurance before the film and examination. It is unsafe and patients recognise it.
items.fix: Honest probability: “Everything so far points away from leukaemia, and here is how we’ll confirm that.”

items.fail: Brushing past the baby and the 2am search to get to the questions.
items.why: The fear for her baby is the hidden agenda. Missing it costs Relating to Others marks and she won’t hear your explanation.
items.fix: “What did you read that frightened you most?” — then name the fear before you explain.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if you’re worried.”
items.why: Non-specific. With platelets of 38 she needs to know exactly which bleeding symptoms are an emergency.
items.fix: Name them: bleeding that won’t stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, severe headache, confusion or weakness — 999 or A&E.

items.fail: Forgetting the heavy periods that prompted the test.
items.why: Low platelets may be causing them, and they are a bleeding risk. Missing the link looks like a checklist history.
items.fix: Ask about flooding and clots, link it to the platelets, and ask haematology how best to treat it.
